paragraphs: AdaVideoRAG addresses a practical problem in answering questions about long videos: different questions need different amounts of context and reasoning. Recognizing an object in one frame may require little retrieval, while connecting events across a video can require several linked pieces of evidence. A fixed retrieval procedure can therefore waste computation or miss important information.

The framework uses a lightweight intent classifier to select a retrieval approach according to query complexity. Its indexing module organizes information from video into several complementary resources: a text database containing clip captions, speech transcriptions, and recognized on-screen text; a visual database; and a graph representing deeper semantic relationships. These resources support access ranging from simple retrieval to more involved graph-based reasoning.

The authors also introduce HiVU, a benchmark for evaluating deeper video understanding. Their experiments report improvements in both accuracy and efficiency for long-video question answering. The framework connects to existing multimodal language models through lightweight API calls, making adaptive retrieval a way to extend their access to video context.
neurips-2025-adavideorag-omni-contextual.tldr: AdaVideoRAG adapts retrieval complexity to each video question, improving long-video question-answering accuracy and efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Language models can evaluate generated answers, but their judgments may reflect preferences for length, presentation order, popular opinions, or emotional tone. Asking evaluators to reconsider their own biases may be insufficient, while directly fine-tuning an evaluator is not always possible. This paper introduces an external Reasoning-based Bias Detector, or RBD, to help correct such judgments.

RBD checks an evaluation for bias and produces structured reasoning that guides the evaluator toward a revision. Detection and revision can repeat without modifying the evaluator itself. The development pipeline constructs biased examples, gathers supervision, and fine-tunes the detector using distilled reasoning. The authors train four detector sizes, spanning 1.5 billion to 14 billion parameters.

Experiments cover four bias categories and eight language-model evaluators. RBD-8B improves evaluation accuracy by an average of 18.5% and consistency by 10.9%, with reported advantages over prompting methods and fine-tuned judges. Improvements occur across detector sizes, and additional experiments support generalization across biases and domains. These results support external feedback as a practical route to more reliable automated evaluation.
neurips-2025-any-large-language-model-ca.tldr: An external bias detector supplies reasoning-based feedback that improves language-model judgments across tested evaluators and bias types.

paragraphs: Fraud detection on graphs depends on recognizing relationships among entities, including connections that are indirect or deliberately concealed. Detectors that mainly examine an entity and its immediate neighbors can overlook longer chains of association. This paper develops Graph Path Aggregation, or GPA, to bring those broader structural relationships into the detection process.

GPA samples paths of varying lengths, encodes their associated meaning, and models interactions among paths before combining their information. The resulting aggregate supports the final fraud decision. This sequence lets evidence from multiple connected entities contribute to detection, including associations that would be difficult to capture through a narrow neighborhood alone.

The authors also create the synthetic G-Internet benchmark to support interpretable analysis of internet-fraud associations. Across datasets representing multiple fraud scenarios, GPA improves Average Precision by up to 15% over mainstream detectors. It also shows stronger robustness to noisy labels. Its interpretability comes from exposing implicit fraud patterns across broader contexts, connecting detection performance with the relationships that help explain suspicious activity.
neurips-2025-association-focused-path-ag.tldr: GPA combines information from graph paths to detect concealed fraud associations, improving precision and robustness in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Text-guided image editing with diffusion models often depends on several interacting settings, including inversion timesteps and attention modifications. Finding a useful combination through repeated trial runs can require substantial computation. AutoEdit treats choosing these settings as part of the editing process itself, aiming to reduce the burden of manually searching a large configuration space.

The method formulates hyperparameter selection as sequential decision-making during diffusion denoising. A reinforcement learning system chooses adjustments across denoising steps, with an explicit Markov decision process organizing those choices. Editing objectives enter through a reward function, so the learned decisions are directed toward the desired editing outcome. The framework uses proximal policy optimization to learn this control behavior.

Experiments report substantial reductions in search time and computational overhead compared with brute-force tuning. The contribution is an automatic mechanism for coordinating interdependent editing settings as generation unfolds. This matters for practical image editing because the cost of finding settings can otherwise become a major part of the cost of producing an acceptable result.
neurips-2025-autoedit-automatic-hyperpar.tldr: AutoEdit uses reinforcement learning to adjust diffusion-editing hyperparameters during denoising, reducing tuning time and computation in experiments.

paragraphs: Connecting a text-based language model to information from another modality usually requires additional supervised training. That requirement makes it harder to adapt immediately to a new domain or representation. This paper investigates whether a language model can instead use representations from other foundation models through examples supplied at inference time.

The proposed proof of concept is In-Context Representation Learning, or ICRL. Ordinary in-context learning presents examples pairing text inputs with labels. ICRL substitutes foundation-model representations for those text inputs, allowing the language model to use non-text information without fine-tuning. The central question is whether a few examples can establish a useful relationship between these representations and the requested output.

The authors evaluate the approach on molecular-domain tasks. Their study examines how representations can be mapped into language models without additional training, which factors affect performance, and what mechanisms explain effectiveness. The contribution establishes a promising direction for adaptable multimodal inference, with the evidence framed as a molecular case study and proof of concept.
neurips-2025-can-llms-reason-over-non-te.tldr: ICRL explores using few-shot examples to let text-based language models work with non-text representations without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: A unified multimodal model combines the ability to understand multimodal inputs with the ability to generate content. This paper investigates whether reinforcement learning can strengthen both capabilities within a shared optimization framework. Its pilot studies suggest that the two abilities can develop together beneficially, motivating a training procedure that explicitly coordinates their improvement.

The proposed CoRL framework uses group relative policy optimization and divides reinforcement learning into two stages. The first jointly optimizes understanding and generation, creating an opportunity for improvements across tasks to support one another. The second refines performance for individual tasks. This structure gives shared learning and task-specific enhancement separate roles within the overall training process.

The resulting model, ULM-R1, achieves average improvements of 7% across three text-to-image generation datasets and 23% across nine multimodal understanding benchmarks. These reported gains support the effectiveness of the combined procedure on both capability groups. They also provide empirical evidence that reinforcement learning can help coordinate understanding and generation within a unified model.
neurips-2025-co-reinforcement-learning-f.tldr: CoRL combines joint and task-specific reinforcement learning to improve both image generation and multimodal understanding in a unified model.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether training a one-hidden-layer ReLU network reaches a global solution when the data points interact weakly. Training is analyzed through gradient flow, a continuous-time description of gradient-based optimization. The analysis uses high-dimensional input geometry and the low correlations between samples that arise in the setting under study.

The main result shows that a hidden-layer width on the order of log(n) is sufficient for global convergence with high probability on n data points. This is a sufficiency result: it establishes that this width can work under the analyzed conditions. A Polyak–Łojasiewicz viewpoint along the training trajectory yields exponential convergence with a rate proportional to 1/n.

For exactly orthogonal data, the authors obtain a more detailed picture. They place the asymptotic convergence rate between orders 1/n and 1/√n and identify a transition from the slower to the faster scale. The relative duration of that transition is on the order of 1/log(n), showing how data geometry can shape the evolution of training speed.
neurips-2025-convergence-of-the-gradient.tldr: For weakly interacting data, the analysis shows that logarithmic-width shallow ReLU networks can converge globally under gradient flow with high probability.

paragraphs: DesignX automates the creation of optimizers for black-box problems, where limited problem-specific knowledge makes manual algorithm design difficult. The framework separates design into two connected decisions: choosing an algorithm's structure and controlling its hyperparameters. Its aim is to produce an optimizer tailored to a particular problem within seconds after learning how to design algorithms.

The authors build a modular search space containing hundreds of algorithm components drawn from prior research. Two reinforcement learning agents collaborate on structural and parameter choices through a shared training objective. Large-scale meta-training uses 10,000 diverse problem instances, giving the system experience with many optimization situations before it designs an optimizer for a given problem.

The paper reports that, after days of autonomous learning, generated optimizers outperform human-designed alternatives by orders of magnitude in the studied settings. Evaluations include synthetic problems, protein docking, AutoML, and UAV path planning. Further analysis identifies nontrivial algorithm patterns, suggesting that automated design can also produce useful insights into how optimization components work together.
neurips-2025-designx-human-competitive-a.tldr: DesignX uses cooperating reinforcement learning agents to assemble problem-specific optimizers, reporting large gains over human-designed alternatives in tested settings.

paragraphs: Expert demonstrations can contain several valid strategies for accomplishing the same task. An imitation learner that compresses these demonstrations into a single behavior loses part of what the experts show. DPAIL addresses this problem by using a diffusion model as its policy, giving the learner a more expressive way to represent multiple behavior modes.

The method builds on Adversarial Soft Advantage Fitting, which removes the need for separate policy optimization steps. DPAIL trains its diffusion policy with a binary cross-entropy objective that distinguishes expert trajectories from generated trajectories. To make this training tractable, the authors derive a lower bound on the policy's likelihood that can be optimized within the framework.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that DPAIL captures diverse behaviors and remains robust as the number of behavior modes increases. The findings support the combination of an expressive diffusion policy with an adversarial training objective that avoids a separate policy optimization stage. The main benefit is preserving the variety present in demonstrations while keeping the learning formulation workable.
neurips-2025-dpail-training-diffusion-po.tldr: DPAIL learns diverse expert behaviors with a diffusion policy trained adversarially, without requiring separate policy optimization steps.

paragraphs: Video anomaly detection needs to identify abnormal moments, but detailed annotations are expensive and weaker labels can be noisy or imprecise. This paper proposes supervising each abnormal video with just one annotated abnormal frame. That frame provides a precise reference while keeping annotation demands low, creating a starting point for learning the broader abnormal event.

The accompanying Frame-guided Progressive Learning method first estimates how strongly other video content relates to the annotated anomaly using evidential learning. It then expands supervision by finding discrete abnormal events through those relevance estimates and feature similarity. The method also separates distinct normal frames outside abnormal events, helping it model normal behavior and reduce false alarms.

The authors manually re-annotate ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, and XD-Violence to create three benchmarks for this supervision setting. Experiments report state-of-the-art detection results and a favorable balance between performance and annotation cost. The central finding is that a small amount of precise frame-level supervision can support learning that extends to complete events.
neurips-2025-generalizing-single-frame-s.tldr: A single labeled abnormal frame guides progressive learning of whole anomalous events, delivering strong detection with limited annotation.

paragraphs: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent limits individual samples' gradient contributions and adds noise during training. Choosing the clipping threshold strongly affects the balance between privacy and model performance. GeoClip focuses on an additional issue: gradient coordinates can be correlated, so adjusting a threshold in the original coordinate system does not fully account for the distribution's geometry.

The framework transforms gradients into a basis aligned with that geometry before clipping and perturbing them. It estimates the transformation adaptively from noisy gradients that have already been released. Consequently, learning this transformation incurs no additional privacy cost. The approach changes how clipping and noise interact with the gradient distribution while using the available private training history.

The authors provide convergence guarantees and a closed-form optimal transformation for minimizing added noise while controlling the probability of clipping. Experiments on tabular and image datasets show consistent improvements over existing adaptive clipping methods at the same privacy budget. These results support accounting for correlations as a useful part of private optimization.
neurips-2025-geoclip-geometry-aware-clip.tldr: GeoClip adapts private gradient clipping to gradient geometry, improving performance at the same privacy budget in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Perturbation-based explanations examine how a model responds when its inputs are changed. Their reliability therefore depends on model behavior under the particular changes used for explanation. This paper studies uncertainty calibration in that setting: whether the model's reported confidence corresponds to its actual accuracy on those perturbed inputs.

The authors find systematic problems in probability estimates under explanation-specific perturbations. They also theoretically establish that this miscalibration undermines both local explanations, which concern individual predictions, and global explanations, which describe broader model behavior. The connection makes confidence quality part of explanation quality, since an explanation can inherit errors from the probabilities it uses.

The proposed ReCalX method recalibrates models for explanation purposes while preserving their original predictions. Evaluations across multiple models and datasets report effective reductions in perturbation-specific miscalibration, alongside more robust explanations and better identification of globally important features. The results indicate that improving the confidence estimates used during explanation can improve transparency without requiring changes to the model's original decisions.
neurips-2025-improving-perturbation-base.tldr: ReCalX improves perturbation-based explanations by recalibrating model confidence while preserving original predictions.

paragraphs: Long-context language-model inference requires retaining information about earlier tokens in a key-value cache, which can strain memory budgets. KeyDiff decides what to retain using similarity among keys. Its starting observation is that geometrically distinctive keys tend to receive high attention scores, suggesting that diversity can help identify important tokens.

The method requires no training and does not directly depend on attention scores. The authors provide a theoretical connection between key diversity and attention, supporting similarity as a basis for eviction. Avoiding attention-score dependence also permits optimized attention implementations such as FlashAttention. The framework is designed to process arbitrarily long prompts within strict resource constraints.

On LongBench, the reported gap from a non-evicting baseline is below 0.04% for two tested Llama models with an 8K cache budget, corresponding to roughly 23% cache reduction. A distilled reasoning model also stays near baseline on Math500. Compared with other eviction methods, end-to-end inference latency falls by up to 30%, supporting the practical value of this retention rule.
neurips-2025-keydiff-key-similarity-base.tldr: KeyDiff uses key similarity to evict cached tokens, reducing memory and latency while staying near baseline performance in reported tests.

paragraphs: MoonCast converts text sources into long, conversational podcasts using voices of unseen speakers. The paper addresses two difficulties that arise beyond short speech synthesis: maintaining coherent interactions across several minutes and producing the spontaneous qualities of spoken dialogue. Those qualities include hesitations and pauses that formal written text often leaves implicit.

For long audio, the system scales a language model's parameters, data, and context and uses a sequence format designed to represent complete multi-speaker, multi-turn interactions. For spontaneity, it draws on the observation that automatic speech recognition transcripts can preserve filler words and textual cues associated with breathing pauses. The authors treat these transcripts as a partial indicator of spontaneous speech.

A script-generation module incorporates such elements into the text that drives synthesis. Experiments report improvements over baselines in contextual coherence and spontaneity. The approach connects long interaction modeling with script preparation, addressing both the continuity of a podcast and the spoken details that make its delivery sound less like a reading of formal prose.
neurips-2025-mooncast-high-quality-zero-.tldr: MoonCast combines long-form speech modeling with scripts containing spontaneous speech cues to generate podcasts in unseen speakers' voices.

paragraphs: This paper develops a more general way to learn transformations between probability distributions. Flow and diffusion models describe such transformations through dynamics indexed by time. The proposed framework expands that organizing variable, allowing vectors, matrices, or linear operators to take the place of a single scalar time value.

This change generalizes stochastic interpolants and allows the framework to bridge distributions across multiple dimensional spaces. The resulting operator-based construction provides a shared theoretical perspective on existing generative models while extending the kinds of transformations they can express. Its practical aim is a generative model that supports multiple tasks without needing separate training specialized to each one.

Numerical experiments demonstrate zero-shot use for conditional generation and inpainting, fine-tuning and posterior sampling, and multiscale modeling. These examples test whether one framework can support different ways of working with distributions. The reported results suggest potential for a broadly applicable alternative to specialized models, with the evidence grounded in the demonstrated tasks rather than a universal guarantee of task independence.
neurips-2025-multitask-learning-with-sto.tldr: Operator-based stochastic interpolants generalize flow and diffusion dynamics to support several generative tasks without task-specific training.

paragraphs: This paper asks how data distributions or language-model representations can be changed so that optimal predictions satisfy exact group-fairness criteria. It defines an ideal distribution as one where minimizing any cost-sensitive risk produces group-fair outcomes, such as demographic parity or equal opportunity. Within that definition, fairness does not require sacrificing the utility captured by the risk.

The authors formulate steering as finding the ideal distribution closest to the original distribution in KL-divergence. This makes the desired fairness property an explicit target while measuring how much the distribution changes. They provide efficient algorithms for familiar parametric distribution families, including normal and log-normal distributions.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets improve fairness without reducing utility, and sometimes improve utility as well. Applications include affine transformations of language-model representations for occupation prediction from biographies and steering representations toward outputs that work equally well across groups. The theoretical guarantee belongs to the defined ideal distributions, while the experiments show how the steering approach behaves in the studied applications.
neurips-2025-on-optimal-steering-to-achi.tldr: The paper finds nearby distributions designed to guarantee exact group fairness and demonstrates steering methods that improve fairness without observed utility loss.

paragraphs: This paper uses shortest-path problems in layered graphs to investigate what makes reasoning traces useful for training language models. The controlled setting separates computational efficiency from the structure of the explanation. Decoder-only transformers learn from question, reasoning-trace, and answer triples, allowing the authors to compare different valid ways of reaching a solution.

One training condition uses optimal bottom-up dynamic programming traces. Another uses longer traces that include backtracking. With the same overall training-token budget, models trained on the longer backtracking traces generalize better to unseen graphs. This result shows that the most efficient solution procedure need not provide the most effective training sequence in this setting.

The advantage does not follow from extra length alone: arbitrary redundancy fails to help and can reduce performance. Instead, generalization correlates with confidence in predicting the next token. The authors interpret this as evidence that coherent, locally incremental reasoning can make learning easier to optimize, even when the underlying solution process uses more steps.
neurips-2025-on-the-bias-of-next-token-p.tldr: In a shortest-path study, longer coherent backtracking traces improve generalization over optimal traces, while arbitrary redundancy does not.

paragraphs: This paper studies online learning of feedforward networks with sign activations, where a learner's performance is measured by mistakes across an input sequence. Inputs lie in a d-dimensional unit ball and outputs belong to a finite label set. The authors identify a sufficient learnability condition: every first-layer neuron separates all inputs with a positive margin bounded away from zero.

That condition is also necessary in some cases. The optimal mistake bound is characterized approximately by a geometric quantity called the totally-separable-packing number, with a matching construction that forces any learner to make that many mistakes. For some networks and input sequences, mistakes can grow exponentially with dimension, making dimension-independent guarantees generally unavailable without further restrictions.

The paper then studies two restrictions that remove dependence on ambient dimension. If the network depends on only s orthonormal directions, the bound is approximately (1.5/γ)^(s+2). If every neuron in every layer has a positive margin, the bound instead depends on label count, margin, and network depth. These results identify structure that can make online learning more manageable.
neurips-2025-online-learning-of-neural-n.tldr: The paper characterizes margin-based online learnability for sign-activation networks and identifies restrictions that avoid dimension-dependent mistake bounds.

paragraphs: Boltzmann generators use learned transformations and importance weighting to sample equilibrium distributions of molecular systems. Flow matching has made continuous normalizing flows more practical by improving speed, supporting more complex systems, and shortening integration trajectories. This paper asks whether further training can improve sampling efficiency while retaining the useful structure learned through flow matching.

The proposed approach fine-tunes a flow-matching-trained model using path gradients. It applies in a setting where the target energy is known, providing information for the refinement stage. The study combines an initial training method that builds efficient flows with a subsequent gradient-based adjustment aimed at improving sampling from the desired molecular distribution.

Experiments show up to a threefold increase in sampling efficiency using the same model and a similar computational budget, without additional sampling. The authors also measure flow-trajectory lengths during fine-tuning and find that path gradients largely preserve the learned flow structure. This supports the hybrid approach as a way to improve sampling while retaining benefits of the original training.
neurips-2025-path-gradients-after-flow-m.tldr: When target energy is known, path-gradient fine-tuning improves molecular sampling efficiency by up to threefold after flow matching.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a language model's size and inference cost, but removing components can also damage performance. Restoration often uses parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods originally designed for dense models. This paper develops a restoration strategy around the specific information lost through pruning, using changes in attention activations to locate what needs compensation.

RestoreLCC first probes important attention heads through contrastive activation editing. It then extracts lost components from differences in activations and injects those components into the corresponding heads of the pruned model. The procedure targets the consequences of pruning directly, using internal activity to identify and compensate for information that the smaller model no longer represents adequately.

The method supports structured, semi-structured, and unstructured pruning. Experiments report consistent advantages over state-of-the-art restoration baselines for both general capabilities and task-specific performance, while preserving sparsity and inference efficiency. The findings suggest that targeted compensation in attention activations can recover useful behavior without giving up the computational benefits that motivated pruning.
neurips-2025-restoring-pruned-large-lang.tldr: RestoreLCC compensates for pruning-related losses in attention activations, recovering model performance while preserving sparsity and inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Generative modeling commonly separates the choice of a noise distribution from the transformation that turns noise into data. This paper explores linking both choices through one convex function. Its starting point is moment measures, which connect sampling from a log-concave distribution with mapping samples through the gradient of the function defining that distribution.

The authors find that the direct moment-measure construction behaves poorly for practical purposes on simple examples, including Gaussians and one-dimensional distributions. They instead propose conjugate moment measures: sampling uses a convex potential w, while the mapping uses the gradient of its convex conjugate. This alternative gives more intuitive behavior on the examples they study.

The resulting mapping is an optimal transport map between the sampling distribution and the target. The authors use optimal transport solvers to learn the potential from target samples and represent it with an input-convex neural network. They also propose a learning algorithm for targets whose density is known only up to a normalizing constant, extending the construction to another common sampling setting.
neurips-2025-sample-and-map-from-a-singl.tldr: Conjugate moment measures link a generator's sampling distribution and transport map through a single learned convex potential.

paragraphs: Models can fail when their deployment data differs from training data because they rely on features that lack a direct causal relationship with the target. Test-time Adaptation by Causal Trimming, or TACT, addresses this problem using unlabeled samples from the target distribution. It adapts predictions by removing representation components associated with non-causal variation.

TACT applies augmentations designed to preserve causal features while changing non-causal ones. It examines the resulting representation changes with Principal Component Analysis and identifies directions with the highest variance. Under this augmentation design, those directions are associated with non-causal features. The method removes representations' projections onto them and makes predictions using the trimmed representations.

As adaptation continues, TACT tracks and refines the selected directions to improve its estimate of non-causal variation. The authors theoretically analyze the approach and evaluate it on real-world out-of-distribution benchmarks, reporting consistent, significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The mechanism depends on augmentations that distinguish the unwanted variation from features that should remain useful for prediction.
neurips-2025-test-time-adaptation-by-cau.tldr: TACT uses causal-feature-preserving augmentations to identify and remove non-causal representation directions during test-time adaptation.

paragraphs: Time-series segmentation divides temporal data into meaningful segments, but evaluating the resulting segments requires more than checking individual change points. The paper argues that existing measures can obscure where errors occur and what kinds of errors were made. A single score may therefore give limited insight into the quality of the detected temporal structure.

The authors introduce two evaluation measures. Weighted Adjusted Rand Index, or WARI, extends ARI to account for the temporal positions of segmentation errors. State Matching Score, or SMS, distinguishes and scores four fundamental error types. SMS also permits different weights for different error types, allowing the evaluation to reflect their relative importance.

Tests on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that the measures provide a more informative assessment of segmentation quality and reveal error type and provenance that traditional measures miss. The contribution is an improved way to assess segmentation outputs and understand their failures. It makes evaluation more useful for diagnosing what a method gets wrong, alongside comparing overall performance.
neurips-2025-toward-interpretable-evalua.tldr: WARI and SMS evaluate time-series segmentation using error location and error type, making quality assessments more interpretable.

paragraphs: This paper quantifies uncertainty when a ranking algorithm orders a combined collection of known and new items. The true relative ordering of n original items is available, but the positions of m new items are unknown. The goal is to provide uncertainty sets for ranks within the full collection of n+m items.

The difficulty is that adding new items also changes the original items' absolute ranks. Their known relative ordering therefore does not directly provide the calibration information needed by ordinary conformal prediction. The authors address this by constructing distribution-free bounds on unknown conformity scores, drawing on results about the distribution of conformal p-values.

Upper bounds on those scores yield valid prediction sets for individual ranks. The method also controls the false coverage proportion, addressing errors across multiple prediction sets rather than only one at a time. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate efficiency with ranking algorithms including RankNet and LambdaMart. The result adds uncertainty information around a black-box ranking without requiring its full ground-truth ordering.
neurips-2025-transductive-conformal-infe.tldr: The method constructs conformal uncertainty sets for full rankings when only the relative ordering of a subset of items is known.

paragraphs: Multivariate forecasting requires capturing how each variable changes over time and how variables relate to one another. xLSTM-Mixer combines temporal modeling, joint time-and-variable information, and multiple perspectives within one forecasting model. Its design brings recurrent modeling together with a mixing architecture to handle these connected sources of structure.

The model begins with a linear forecast shared across variables. xLSTM blocks then refine that initial forecast to account for more complex dynamics. The architecture ultimately reconciles two distinct views to produce its final prediction. This gives the initial forecast and subsequent recurrent processing complementary roles, with the refinement stage handling patterns beyond the shared linear starting point.

Extensive evaluations report stronger long-term forecasting performance than recent state-of-the-art methods while requiring very little memory. The authors also analyze the model's components and report evidence of robustness and effectiveness. These results support recurrent models combined with mixing architectures as a useful design direction for accurate forecasting under modest memory requirements.
neurips-2025-xlstm-mixer-multivariate-ti.tldr: xLSTM-Mixer refines shared linear forecasts with recurrent mixing blocks, reporting strong long-term multivariate forecasting with low memory use.
